In 2002, under OECD pressure, Gibraltar announced its intended abolition of the tax-exempt company and the introduction of a new corporate taxation policy setting a zero rate of corporation tax for all companies but introducing new taxes on company personnel and property occupation which would be capped at 15% of profits. However, in 2004, the EU challenged such a regime on the basis, inter alia, that since the taxes were based on payroll and the occupation of business premises, offshore companies registered in Gibraltar would be unlikely to incur any tax liability. The issue rumbled on, however, since the Income Tax Act 2010, a Gibraltarian ‘ordinarily resident company’ pays corporate income tax at 10% on worldwide income; whereas a ‘non-resident company’ pays at a nil rate. An ordinary resident company is defined as: i. a company the management and control of whose business is exercised in Gibraltar; or ii. a company which carries on business in Gibraltar and the management and control of which is exercised outside Gibraltar; or iii. an investment company which is domiciled anywhere outside Gibraltar, where control of the company, through shares or voting powers, is exercised by persons ordinarily resident in Gibraltar. A non-resident company is defined as a company that is incorporated in Gibraltar and does not trade or earn income in Gibraltar. The dichotomy persists.

46. Many commentators consider Hong Kong to be an offshore tax haven. While its tax rates are low by OECD standards, and a number of the taxes that are imposed by most onshore jurisdictions do not exist in Hong Kong (so there is no CGT, withholding tax, sales tax and no accumulated earning taxes on companies that retain earnings rather than distributing them), it is not a ‘tax haven’ in the traditional sense in that it does not confer tax exemption upon non-resident companies. Instead, it imposes taxes according to the territorial principle, i.e. taxes are only levied upon income derived from or arising within Hong Kong and not on income generated from a source located outside the Territory. While unsophisticated, this does not offend the international community by ring fencing – a tax regime which is considered to be improper and unfair in a global context. See Appendix 6B section 7.

2. Terminology can be confusing. A ‘public company’ may issue shares to the general public by way of a public offering, but it is not required to do so; accordingly, a public company may sell shares on a private basis or at a public offering. A ‘publicly traded company’ has actually issued shares to the public. A ‘listed company’ is a public company that has issued shares to the public, and these shares are listed, and can therefore be traded, on a stock exchange. A ‘private company’, on the other hand, cannot make an offer to sell its shares to the public by way of public offering: it can only offer to sell its shares to an identified individual or small group on a private basis. 10. Unfortunately there are serious flaws in the theory. The authorised share capital of a company is a meaningless figure. The authorised share capital may be shown in the memorandum as $1 million, but if only two $1 shares are issued the actual capital, namely the critical figure representing the amount available for creditors, is only $2! A more meaningful requirement to adequately protect creditors would be for a company to be obliged to have a minimum share capital before it can commence business. But there is no such requirement. And if there were, the minimum capital requirement would operate when the company is formed, not when it is needed by creditors, namely when the company ceases to trade because it is insolvent. The following is a concise summary of the streamlined procedure for a Jersey company to be wound up on a voluntary basis: • The directors must convene a general meeting of the shareholders for the purpose of passing a special resolution to have the company dissolved. The directors must present a declaration of solvency to the shareholders. • The shareholders meet and, if appropriate, pass the special resolution. • The directors, officers and members prepare a letter addressed to the registrar confirming that they wish the company to be dissolved. • When corporate income tax was payable, the directors had to obtain confirmation from the local tax offices that there was no tax liability outstanding, but this is now superfluous as Jersey companies pay a nil rate of tax. • Copies of the letters from the directors, officers, members are sent to the registrar of companies with a request to have the company dissolved. • Notices must be published in the local press recording the company’s wish to be dissolved. • Providing no objections are received, the registrar of companies will remove the company from the Register after a stipulated period of three months has passed.

229. This part of the text describes the rule in Dearle v Hall (1828) 3 Russ 1: that the first in time prevails. The issue of priority between successive charges is actually a little more complex. This is because in English company law one must distinguish between the date of the charge and the date of its registration in the register of charges. Under early companies legislation in England, starting with the 1862 Act, through 1900, 1948, 1985 right up to the 2006 Companies Act, particulars of every fixed and floating charge made by a company must be entered into the company’s register of charges. Failure to register does not invalidate the charge, but it may affect priority between successive charges. This is because registration serves as constructive notice to subsequent chargees. In short, the priority of successive charges may be governed by the date of registration rather than the date of the instrument creating the charge. To make matters more complex for offshore companies and their advisers, there are a number of jurisdictions where registration is not a mandatory requirement. In such jurisdictions the first in time, rather than the first to be registered, does indeed prevail and has priority over subsequent charges.

The new voluntary striking off procedure created by s.1003 of the Companies Act 2006 permits a company, by board resolution, to apply to the registrar on prescribed Form DS01 for the voluntary removal of the company from the register. A board resolution is required, although for a multi-shareholder company it is likely that the board would obtain the prior approval of the shareholders in general meeting. The application cannot be made if the company is engaged in court proceedings or at any time in the last three months has: traded, made any disposal of its assets or changed its name. Having filed Form DS01 with the registrar, notice is published in the Gazette giving two months for objections. If no objections are received the registrar will strike the company off the register and give a further notice of doing so in the Gazette. At this stage the company is dissolved although can be reinstated by an application to the court within six years of the striking off.
